subject: human brain halves
title: What If Your Brain Were Cut in Two? Surgeons Did It. Few Could Tell

scenes.text: What if your brain were cut in two? Surgeons have done it. Almost nobody could tell.
From the 1940s, surgeons treated severe epilepsy by cutting the corpus callosum, the band of fibers joining the brain's two halves.
Afterwards, patients seemed themselves. No apparent change in personality or intelligence.
Then came the tests. Flash a picture to the left side of vision, which feeds the silent right half. The patient says, I saw nothing. The left hand draws it.
One man struggled to button his shirt. As one hand buttoned, the other unbuttoned.
And when the right half acted alone, the talking left half made up a reason on the spot. Scientists named it the interpreter.

description:
What if the two halves of your brain could no longer talk to each other? Beginning in the 1940s, surgeons cut the corpus callosum to treat severe epilepsy. Patients showed no apparent change in personality, emotion or intelligence.
But experiments by Roger Sperry and Michael Gazzaniga showed the halves working separately: a picture shown only to the right hemisphere could not be named, yet the left hand could draw it, and the speaking left hemisphere invented explanations for the right's actions. Sperry shared the 1981 Nobel Prize. The surgery is very rare today.
